summary: Extends delivery status and disposition notifications to work with internationalized email addresses. Existing specifications limited the machine-readable parts to US-ASCII, so this adds a new address type so that original recipient addresses with non-ASCII characters are preserved correctly. It is experimental and was replaced by RFC 6533.

eli5.summary: When a letter bounces, the notice should name the address properly. This lets bounce messages cope with addresses written in other alphabets. It was replaced by RFC 6533.

subtitle: Delivery status notifications that preserve non-ASCII email addresses.

tldr.problem: When mail bounces or is undelivered, the notification message is supposed to show the original recipient address. But the existing delivery status notification (DSN) format only supports ASCII text, losing information about addresses written in non-ASCII alphabets.
tldr.mechanism: This specification adds a new UTF-8 address type with three encoding forms (xtext, unitext, and native), and three new MIME types (message/global-delivery-status, message/global-headers, and message/global-disposition-notification) to carry internationalized addresses in bounce and disposition notifications.
tldr.outcome: Mail systems can now preserve the original recipient address even after downgrading, and can generate bounce messages that accurately reflect addresses in any language.

today: RFC 5337 is Experimental and was obsoleted by RFC 6533, which standardized internationalized DSN and MDN handling. Modern mail systems use the standardized approach for preserving international addresses in notifications.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 5337 extends delivery status notifications (DSNs) and message disposition notifications (MDNs) to work with internationalized email addresses. DSNs are the automatic bounce messages that mail servers send when a message cannot be delivered. The RFC solves a critical problem: when an internationalized message is undeliverable, the bounce notification should preserve the original recipient address so that the sender can understand which address failed.

The companion RFC 5336 enables mail servers to send messages with UTF-8 addresses, but those messages sometimes fail to deliver. RFC 5337 ensures that when such failures occur, the notification preserves the international address accurately, even when the message must pass through systems that do not fully support UTF-8.
sections.eli5: When something goes wrong with email delivery, the system sends back a notice saying what went wrong and to whom. This spec makes sure that notice includes the actual address that failed, even if it uses non-English letters.

sections.title: UTF-8 Address Types
sections.content:
The RFC introduces a new address type for use in delivery and disposition notifications: the UTF-8 address type. This type has three different encoding forms depending on the context. The utf-8-address form uses native UTF-8 characters and is suitable for messages with UTF-8 headers. The utf-8-addr-unitext form encodes problematic characters so the address can pass through systems that require 7-bit data. The utf-8-addr-xtext form is fully 7-bit-safe and uses xtext encoding from RFC 3461, suitable for SMTP ORCPT parameters.

The RFC also defines an EmbeddedUnicodeChar syntax using the \x{HEXPOINT} notation to represent Unicode code points in hexadecimal. This provides a transitional mechanism for systems that cannot yet handle native UTF-8. As systems evolve, the expectation is that the native UTF-8 forms will become standard.
sections.eli5: The same international address can be written three different ways depending on where it will be sent. Some systems can handle UTF-8 directly, others need a special encoding. This spec handles all three cases.

sections.title: Internationalized Delivery Status Notifications
sections.content:
When a message is undeliverable, the mail system returns a multipart/report message with three parts: human-readable text, a delivery status body part, and optionally the undeliverable message or its headers. This specification introduces a new media type, message/global-delivery-status, which has the same structure as the traditional message/delivery-status but uses UTF-8 charset instead of ASCII.

The new type allows UTF-8 characters in the Diagnostic-Code field and adds a new optional field called Localized-Diagnostic that can include error messages in multiple languages, each tagged with a language code. Systems SHOULD convert the xtext or unitext forms of addresses in the ORCPT parameter to the native utf-8-address form when placing them in the Original-Recipient field of the global-delivery-status body part.
sections.eli5: When mail bounces, the bounce message is sent in multiple parts: human text, machine-readable status, and optionally the bad message back. The new version of the status part can handle international addresses and languages.

sections.title: Message Disposition Notifications
sections.content:
Message Disposition Notifications (MDNs) are read receipts and other notices that a mail user agent sends in response to received messages. The RFC introduces a new media type, message/global-disposition-notification, alongside the new message/global and message/global-headers types for returning the message or headers themselves. Like delivery status notifications, MDNs can now contain UTF-8 in the failure, error, and warning fields.

The Original-Recipient header field in an MDN, when generated for a UTF-8 header message, should use the utf-8-address form of the UTF-8 address type. The Disposition-Notification-To header, which specifies where to send the MDN, follows the same rules as other address headers in UTF-8 messages.
sections.eli5: Read receipts (when someone confirms they got your message) also get updated. They can now handle international addresses the same way bounce messages do.

sections.title: New MIME Media Types
sections.content:
The RFC formally defines three new MIME media types. message/global-headers carries only the header fields of a UTF-8 message, useful for returning just the headers without the body. message/global-delivery-status carries delivery status information with UTF-8 support as described above. message/global-disposition-notification carries disposition notification information with UTF-8 support.

All three types use 8-bit content transfer encoding when possible. When messages pass through 7-bit-only SMTP infrastructure, base64 or quoted-printable encoding may be applied. The RFC notes that multipart/report containers MUST accept any combination of the traditional (message/delivery-status, message/rfc822, text/rfc822-headers) and new global types interchangeably.
sections.eli5: The system needed new container types to hold the international content. These three new types handle bounce messages, read receipts, and headers in a way that preserves international addresses.
